Assault Pack Design Review:
FILBE vs Kahakka

01 Feb 2026

Propper International FILBE vs Savotta Kahakka
(America vs Europe)

Notice: This is an in-depth gear review of two "military" backpacks. It is detailed, technical and critical. You've been warned.

Article Description: This is a comparative design and quality review of the FILBE Assault Pack (AP), used by the United States Marine Corps (USMC), and the Savotta Kahakka 25L Backpack, a commercial version of the M20 pack used by Finnish Defense Forces (FDF).

This review is not about which pack is superior, nor about providing ratings -- it is about understanding the design, engineering, and build quality of these packs. This review highlights how each could be improved. I attempt to account for the reasoning behind the packs' design choices and if the justifications for these decisions are warranted.

All of my suggested improvements are marked as "FILBE" or "Kahakka Recommendations"

Propper FILBE

Savotta Kahakka

Savotta M20


How do two military assault packs,
one from the USA's defense powerhouse,
the other born from Finland's sisu,
measure up?


While characterizing this as an “Europe vs America” is a bit unfair, It may be unfair because:
1)The Kahakka is made for commercial, not military sale
2) Different manufactures (Propper vs Eagle Industries) may have differing qualities, independent of home country
3) Propper and Savotta don’t make all the backpacks (or equipment) for all of American and Finish armed forces. it is still worthwhile to compare the design considerations and build quality between products fulfilling similar roles across the Atlantic. Some of the noted findings do seem to highlight the cultural and stereotypical differences between the countries (USA vs Finland) in question.

Testing duration: Both of these backpacks have been tested for at least 1 year.

Relevant Experience: No combat experience. Lots of milsim sports experience. Professional background in engineering, design, and user experience.

The principal considerations are:

  1. Everyday Carry Use (EDC)
  2. Combat Usage (CU)
  3. Manufacturing and Quality

I will refer to each pack as the FILBE Typically, FILBE refers to the main rucksack (80L) in the FILBE system, not the assault pack. Here I will just refer to it as the FILBE.and Kahakka from here on.

Summary of differences (the TLDR)

The Very Short of it: The FILBE is bigger and heavier, The FILBE has a larger volume, even if the tech specs say otherwise. capturing the American design ethos. It is also cheaper. The Kahakka is smaller and leaner, demonstrating the European one. The build quality is notably higher, and so is the price.

The Short of it with details: For everyday and short-term combat usage, the design of the FILBE is superior. The FILBE's simple compartment system ensures quick and effective organization. Its J-Zip in particular provides excellent ease-of-access. In contrast, the Kahakka's top flap closure is inconvenient, especially for retrieving items at the bottom of the pack. Furthmore, the hunter's green PU inner lining makes visibility in the main compartment difficult.

For long-term combat usage and poor weather, the Kahakka's design may be better due to its improved protection against the elements -- though it lacks drainage grommets, and whether this is a practical disadvantage is unclear.

The FILBE is more comfortable with heavier loads due to wider, better padded straps. It is cooler on the back because of the dual-channel padding. This later advantage is negated while wearing a plate carrier. For everyday travel, the Kahakka is 0.5 kg lighter. Notably, the actual body height is only 40cm (not the advertised 48cm), meaning if not overstuffed, it meets RyanAir's small bag dimensions (i.e. 40x30x20cm). The FILBE (~51 cm) will require bending if tested.

While aesthetics are mostly opinion, it can affect EDC and how others react to the wearer. The FILBE clearly carries a military air, while the Kahakka less so. I have been prevented from entering certain museums and areas of interest while wearing the FILBE, although this was during the European Terror waves (2015-2017). I think it is less likely I would have been stopped with the Kahakka, but still very possible.

The quality of the Kahakka is simply superior -- both in terms of material and construction. The manufacturing quality of the FILBE has, in my experience (4 different packs!), significantly regressed since its release.

For EDC, where I must access items readily, the FILBE is the clear choice. And I do end up using it more often. For hiking, the decision comes down to season, and carry needs. In hot weather or heavy carry loads, the FILBE is my choice. For cold weather, the choice is equivalent. For general travel where size and weight matters, the Kahakka is betterThe exception to this is if you have a lot of computer equipment to carry, and must it removed at airport security. Item access with the FILBE really is just that much better..

As of 02/2026, I am working on a redesign of my Kahakka based on my experiences, most of which are noted here. I intend to bring it to a tailor (or shoemaker) for modifications, making it more practical. You can find my project details here (NOTE: not yet published).

Introduction and History

If you’re reading this, you likely already have an interest in at least one of these packs. Therefore, I’ll be concise with the history.

The Family of Improved Load Bearing Equipment (FILBE) Assault Pack (AP) was first fielded by the USMC sometime in 2011-2012. As of 02/2026 (time of writing), it is still the AP in service for the USMC. It was produced by both Eagle Industries and Propper International. Only in late 2024 did it become available for consumer purchase from Propper. However, it was available as military surplus as early as 2013-2014.

The Kahakka was released to the consumer market in 2024, making it some 12 years younger. It is based on the the FDF’s M20 pack, with learnings from the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine.

Why I care so much about this (and why it matters to you!)

I had the same backpack for 9 years (RIP 2015-2024). It was used at least as many days as I had it, probably more.

Sometimes it hardly carried anything but papers, other times it was stuffed to the brim, camping gear strapped to the side. It was with me as I rode the métro and walked the streets of Paris to university. It was with me when I reached the foot of the glaciers on Mont Blanc. It’s seen the beaches on both sides of the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. It’s been over the Alps, Appalachians, Blue Stacks and Derryveaghs, and even graced the Lake District. It’s survived a dozen different farms, carried books into at least 4 different universities, and most importantly, had a pocket just for holding a fresh baguette.


That pack was the FILBE

FILBE Assault Pack with a backdrop of Mont Blanc, Europe's tallest mountain.

When you’ve carried something like that for so long, it becomes a part of your identity, and an icon of yourself. Folks recognize you just by its silhouette. When I tested other bags, my friends didn’t like it. “You should get a new one of the same bag,” They said. “It’s like it’s not you anymore.”


And, I didn't really want a new bag


But, unfortunately, after 9 years of wear-and-tear, my original FILBE needed to be replaced. It wasn’t so much the standard usage which got it, but an accident within the first months of purchase. I left it against a radiator in a caravan (that wasn’t supposed to work), waking during the middle of the night to the odor of burning plastic. The melted holes became weak points no patching seemed to resolve (perhaps a fault of my own tailoring skills). Eventually, one huge tear formed at the top of the bag, perpetually letting in rain.

The rip in its final form.


It was time for a new bag -- but which?

Whatever replacement pack came, it would be would have big shoes to fill. My FILBE had been part of my life for just shy of a decade.

Buying a new one seemed the obvious choice. But, a new FILBE direct from Propper would have cost $180 (USD), a frustrating price given how much I originally paid. Used ones could be had for much less. “Like-new” ones however were not acceptably cheaper to risk getting one with holesIt was not possible at the time to physically visit a military surplus store that might have one for physical inspection., likely leading to the same demise as the previous.

So, I thought a lot about getting a new pack, and the right one. Whatever pack came next would have high standards to meet.


Enter the Kahakka


At about this time, I was interested in The Road to Vostok, an indie game (still in the making as of 02/2026) whose fictional Finnish setting somewhat mirrors that of the Chornobyl and Pripyat Exclusion zones in Ukraine. It also at that time that Road to Vostok gained its first commercial collaborator: Savotta. Here’s a short commericial:

Savotta is a well-known Finnish supplier of outdoor gear, for both military, police, and recreational use in “extreme-environments.”

"We are Savotta and we make military gear"


If that clip doesn't convince you to buy one of their products (or want to be Finnish),
well then, you're clearly not me.


Although it was more expensive than purchasing a new FILBE, I decided to take the plunge. I purchased my Kahakka for €185 or $205 (purchased at 10% discount) back in October of 2024 . In the end, I would also end up purchasing a new FILBE for the price of $180 just a few months later.

First Impressions

The first time I saw the Kahakka, side by side with the FILBE, I thought,

"…and this is the difference between America and Europe."

Front View - 2014 FILBE and 2024 Kahakka

Right Side View – Hole on top of the FILBE is partly visible

Top-Front View – The hole in the top of the FILBE is partly visible

Back View – Age related fraying on the FILBE is visible

Traveling between the USA and Europe tends to result in what I call “aspect ratio shock.” — a sensation that everything has been visually stretched. It’s akin to changing the aspect ratio on your TV or monitor from 4:3 to 16:10 in an instant (or vice versa) - just with real life.

Go from Europe to America and the world feels flattened and stretched wide. A “single lane” in American suburbia feels equivalent to a rural double lane in the European countryside. Come back to continental Europe and everything is tall and narrow, from ceiling heights to light posts. More generally, American products are heavier, bulkier, and more comfortable. European products are lighter, more economical, and spartan.

There are a lot of examples of this aspect-ratio and product differences between Europe and the USA. Consider the difference between American and European printing paper formats. Americans love their "short and fat" 8.5″x10″ sheets, and Europeans their 8.3″x11.7″.

Regarding products, cars are a perfect example, even from the same manufacturer. American cars are larger. Even when comparing the same car model, just between continents, American suspensions are softer. While European products are trimmed, this also means they're fitted.

You can also observe this in how the average person dresses in Europe versus the USA. Europeans are better dressed. They tend to wear tight, hemmed clothes, pants that aren't jeans, and aren't necessarily blue (or black or khaki), sweaters over their button up long-sleeve shirts, and nice shoes. Each pair of socks they own are unique. Not dozens of pairs of the same exact sock. And well… Americans, they wear that one-size-fits-all from Costco, baggy jeans, and if they're an older father, those "classic" 608 V5s (because well, they are comfortable).

As an experiment, I gave Nano Banana Pro the following image generation prompt: "Imagine me stereotypical images of American man average clothing and average European"



And that is the FILBE vs Kahakka in a nutshell.
The FILBE is baggy, spacious, heavy, but more comfortable. It is a brute of a bag.
The Kahakka is thin, tight, and light. It is a precise pack.


Pack Anatomy

Each aspect of the packs will be reviewed and compared in this section:

  1. Main Compartment (access, organization)
  2. Pouches and Pockets
  3. Straps and Buckles (Shoulder, Hip, Buckle types)
  4. Back Panel

Build quality is discussed later, but mentioned where specifically appropriate.

Two terms worth highlighting are Single Handed Usage (SHU) and Fine Motor Control (FMC). These are important concepts in military gear applications (to me) because they determine how readily a product can be used when injured (single handed usage case) and/or when under extreme stress where fine motor control becomes reduced and usability a premium requirement.

Main Compartment

Main Compartment Access

The Main Compartment is the heart of every pack. Access to this on the Kahakka is through a fold top lid secured by 2 side release (SR) buckles. The female ends of these buckles have flared entrances, similar to a flared magwell on firearms. This is the first time I’ve seen this on an SR buckle, though I’m sure they exist elsewhere. It’s a clever inclusion – it does make buckling easier, especially in stressful situations where fine motor control goes out this window.

Front of pack with 2 SR buckles and their flared inserts.

In comparison, the FILBE uses a J-zip, so named because the zipper is stretches longer down one side than the other.

FILBE (2025) Main Compartment Access - Long side of the 'J-zip'

The Kahakka’s main compartment is easier to open. It only requires one hand to unlatch the SR buckles, and lift the lid. But this is only part of the story to main compartment access. In comparison, the FILBE has a two-way zip, but neither of these move freely enough without some additional force on the pack to hold it in place. Although opening the compartment is more challenging, compartment access is still better on the FILBE.

Why is this the case?

Because the Kahakka uses a fold top lid. This system is great because it eliminates the weaknesses of zippers while leveraging the pack’s shell to keep out the elements. Fold top lids are common in recreational hiking packs. But, they are not they the right choice for assault packs.

While opening a fold top lid can be done single handed, the system doesn’t provide easy access to materials in the comparment, except those placed at the top. It is a “last in, first out” system. To worsen this, when the fold top lid opens, the folded prtion becomes an extended neck. In effect, the pack becomes a longer tube. Even for a short pack like this, bottom access is challenging.

My arm length is typical to that of a 6’ or 183cm tall man. As an EDC example, putting the Kahakka on the cashier’s counter and trying to put in groceries with a semblance of organiation is actually really hard. I ultimately stopped using the Kahakka as an EDC mainly for this reason. I couldn’t get my groceries without struggling.And we know what those Aldi/Lidl cashiers are like!

One solution to bottom compartment access is often found in larger hiking packs with fold top lids. At the bottom, there is a zippered “sleeping bag section.” However, when everything must be packed from bottom-to-top, things will inevitably get pulled out of the pack onto the ground for access. I can’t imagine having to fidget with any of this, fold top lid or even a bag zipper, in combat when some sort of ammunition, medical supply, etc. has made its way to the bottom or some unknown, odd position. For this, the J-Zip on the FILBE is far more convenient.

One redemption of the implementation in the Kahakka’s fold top lid is a plastic insert in the lower lip (towards bottom of picture below). This little flexible piece does the job of keeping the mouth of the lid open and squared. I know it’s a rectangle, but “rectangled” doesn’t read as smoothly as a verb There is a seam on this lower lip which is sharp and seems to catch a lot. I was concerned how this seam would hold up in time, but after more than a year it is no worse for wear.

Plastic Insert on bottom lip keeps opening squared. Seam on bottom is "rough" where there is a 45 degree in the stitching.

Main Compartment Organization

The Kahakka has limited organization in the main compartment – a single pouch for a hydration bladder. The top of the pouch is kept under tension by an internal elastic band. There are 3 togs providing anchors to a bladder.

I am not a fan of elastic tensioning because these materials eventually “dry out,” losing their elasticity and ability to do their job.

There is one particular grievances I have against the Kahakka – its internal PU coating. This is a great idea to increase weather resistance. But, this particular coating is a hunter’s green (i.e. a very, very dark green). I know not if this was intentional, such as a carry over from procurement specifications for the M20. For example, it might be a deliberate decision to reduce any potential of an offending light signature leaking from inside the main compartment at night. But ultimately, this dark coating makes locating anything, even on a sunny day, frustrating.

My constructive advice would be to use a lighter material to reflect light further down the cavity, and if needed, use a darker coating only at the very top, and/or on the outer pouches, for concealment.

Kahakka Organization (photo taken on very sunny mediterranean day). Exposure adjusted to match visible brightness.
Visible: elastic hydration bladder
"Hello darkness my old friend…"

In comparison, the FILBE has simple but effective organization. A single-zippered mesh pocket hangs at the top front. It is very easy to access, even just opening the main J-Zip slightly allows one to see what’s inside due to the mesh covering. This is particularly useful for EDC and travel for items like keys and IDs.

The FILBE features a radio comparment, which can be used to hold a hydration bladder. Unlike the Kahakka, it does not have locking anchors for the bladder, presumably because these would get in the way of the radio. In my own experience with the FILBE and a water bladder, the lack of anchors makes little difference, though I have only tried the wider variety. The radio pouch features a strap with buckle, something which is preferred over the elastic of the Kahakka’s elastic band (i.e. the buckle is not going to wear out).

Both the Kahakka and FILBE have exit slots for water bladder tubes (or radio antennae for the later). I heavily prefer the flap coverings that Savotta has used. They are located on each side of the flip top lid, just above the hemming in my photos, towards the rear of the packs. The exit slots on the FILBE are covered by Velcro and part of the top carrying handle. Despite rarely using these, they show great wear at this stage. Their top placement makes them less than ideal for inclement weather, but this may be a necessity for the intended radios antennas.

The FILBE also features 2 internal side pockets or “canteen” pouches which I have personally named as follows: the “Baguette holder” and the “Grenade pouch”. The “Baguette holder” is the long pocket tube, rising up to the short end of “J-zip.” The “Grenade holder” is on the other side, and has very short walls. It’s not clear to me what either is explicitly for. The Baguette holder, besides holding baguettes, is useful for cables, chargers, bottles, and dongles as an EDC. Concerning baguettes, this shows another benefit of the J-Zipper over a fold-top lid. The J-Zipper can be left partially open, such that objects taller than the height of the pack can be secured in the main compartment (like a baugette), but extend outward. As for the Grenade holder, I’ve found little utility for it except for rolled socks as I’ve yet to find grenades about.

Finally, the FILBE’s main compartment also features a zipper for access to the plastic rear panel, just above the radio pouch. This reveals an additional “compartment.” In the past I’ve used this pouch to store documents and hide back-up cash while traveling as the zipper goes unnoticed. It is strange that a zipper was incorporated here instead of a flap, or even no opening at all as it would’ve likely lowered production cost and weight. If anyone reading this has theories or knowledge about this, I would be pleased to hear it.

FILBE Organizaton (J-Zipper open)
Visible: radio pouch, mesh pocket, baguette holder, and back panel access.

One final note on the main compartments – the Kahakka emplys no drainage grommets while the FILBE utilizes 3 (and 2 for the front pouch). Drainage grommets permit water to escape should it manage to get inside. The Finns and the Marines are focued on rather different geographic sectors. The lack of grommets may be due to the Finnish Defense Forces pack requirements, which again, I am wholly ignorant of, and they may have requested no external openings for drainage. The Finns may prefer the the “Hardshell” philosophy - “Never give water a chance to get in, and you won’t get wet.”

On the otherhand, with the USMC being focused on maritime operations, and taking the “Softshell” philosophy - “You will get wet no matter what, so keep the door open for it to leave” – it’s no surprise that even their hot weather boot has drainage grommets.

Bottom of the FILBE - The FILBE has 5 drainage grommets, 3 in the main compartment (1 visible here, 2 outlines of the others can be seen under the PALS webbing) and 2 in the front pouch.

Bottom of the Kahakka (no grommets)

Main Compartment Sizing

The published specifications describe the Kahakka’s main compartment having a volume of 25L (…well, sort’ve. And we’ll come back to that). On the other hand, the FILBE is described as having a compartment of just 23L (according to Propper’s published dimensions.)

I don’t have the gold standard volume measurement The pack is filled with a countable quantity of 20mm balls to determine the volume. at hand – but I do have eyes which tell me these numbers are fudged. For a start, the FILBE’s main compartment is certainly larger than the Kahakka’s.

Let’s investigate with a ruler, calculator, and some eyes how big these main compartments really are, and where the numbers might be coming from.

Propper describes their volume in the following way, and the volume measurement is derived as follows:

From Propper.com: "20 in. x 14 in. x 5 in. main compartment"

20 × 14 × 5 = 1,400 cubic inches

1 cubic inch is equal to approximately 0.0164 Liters.

1,400 × 0.0164 = 22.96 Liters

Main Compartment ≈ 23 Liters.

A loose remeasuring of the pack arrives at a different figure of 24.6 L (i.e. 48 cm x 32 cm x 16 cm). Given the design of the pack, the figure is likely in the 26-28L range.

How can this be? It is due to the seam type, fabric contouring, and overall shape of the pack. For example, accounting for the observed external contouring on the FILBE’s front alone, results in an increased compartment size calculation above 26L. This is because, while the fabric itself does not stretch, it is able to expand by more than 1cm outward, without causing a compensatory constriction on the sides.

Explicitly, the FILBE uses a hidden stictch seam, which along with the bagginess of the fabric itself, promotes the fabric’s outward expansion. You can see this in the image below where the FILBE’s main compartment is able to “puff out” both on the front, on the top, and on the side. Basically, in every direction.

In constrast, the Kahakka uses an external seam where the fabric points inwards toward the center of the pack. This creates tension when the pack is filled. For the compartment to fill, the fabric must fight against the seam. In the image below we can see the front of the Kahakka bulging which supports the seam in its natural horizontal plane to the front of the bag. This makes the side fabric taut, as it must fold against the seam, and we see less bulging here.

Kahkka with puffed front, tight sides

FILBE puffy all around

To be clear, the seam type does not explain the size discrepancies between packs. It does explain how in combination with the fabric contouring, textiles can produce a greater volume than one might expect, when simply doing volume calculations from dimensions and assuming a rigid shape. Of course all sides of the Kahakka will begin to bulge and expand with sufficient force. No seam type will prevent that.

Loosely remeasuring the Kahakka results in an estimated volume of just 19.1 liters (i.e. 41 cm × 26 cm × 18 cm). So how exactly does Savotta arive at a main compartment measuring of 25L? Well it doesn’t. Savotta doesn’t infact directly claim this. Savotta only says, “Capacity ca. 25 litres (excl. bellowed side pouches).”

But many (maybe most?) vendors and even pack reviewers continue to claim that the main compartment has a volume of 25L. Some examples:

  1. “The main compartment has a capacity of 25 liters.”
  2. “The main compartment offers a 25-liter capacity”
  3. “The capacity is 25 L for the main compartment”
  4. “With a main volume of 25 liters”
  5. “The main compartment offers ~ 25 liters of storage.”

So what is Savotta exactly saying? I’m not sure. I have found 2 ways to arrive at this claim of “Capacity ca. 25 litres (excl. bellowed side pouches)”:

  1. Consider that the “capacity” refers to both the top lid pocket (~3L) and the main compartment partly extended by ~8cm (~3”) to reach 22L (i.e. 3 + 22 = 25L)
  2. Or, consider the “capacity” refers to the main comparment with the top lid’s neck fully extended and the top-lid just covering the opening to arrive at +25.25L

It would be nice if Kahakka specified what they meant. Regardless, this doesn’t affect any opinion I have on either bag. But, I would say this is the key take away:

FILBE Main Compartment: ~27L
Kahakka Main Compartment: 19--25L (depending on neck extension)

Pouches and Pockets

Kahakka

The Kahakka has 2 external zippered pockets, and 2 external side pouches. The first external pocket is part of the folding lid and can be accessed by a double-slider zipper. This zipper has a fabric overhang providing weather protection. The pocket is described as having a “a capacity of ca. 3 litres, suitable for NVDs, water bottles etc.”

However, this estimation seems unrealistic as the pocket feels quite small. I doubt a 2L bottle would fit within. Even without gloves, my hand is always scrapping against the zippers when trying to retrieve items. I imagine this would only be more challenging while wearing gloves during the Finnish winter.

I believe this access and “felt”” volume issue stems from the shape of the pocket, and its shared wall which forms the top of the lid. Tension on the lid from when the pack is closed can make storage and retrieval harder.

The promotional video for the Kahakka 25L shows them pulling out a pair of binoculars. The key to accessing the compartment is therefore by using an additional hand to pull the external layer and top stringerA stringer is the assembly of one side of a zipper. That is, the fabric tape and the attached teeth for either the top or bottom row. upward. This means single handed use is more difficult.

Top Lid Pocket

At first I was quite nervous about putting anything small or important inside, such as keys or ID, because the zipper is close to the bottom of the pocket, and my initial testing found items were likely to spill out. My +1 year of experience though has found this is be less probable than on first appearance, but I am always mindful of the possibility so it may just be caution in practice. In summary, it is the easiest pocket to access on the Kahakka but the least secured.

Kahakka Recommendation: Personally, I would like to see the zipper moved 2-3cm (~1”) higher. This would mean the fabric overhang would start just at the top of the velcro patch on the lid. My redesign Kahakka would also have a zipper on the underside of the top lid flap.

For those wondering, the Medium sized Savotta Rain Cover fits perfectly inside this compartment but consumes nearly all the volume. You can still put some minor items in, but at the risk of them being pulled out unintentionally when retrieving the cover. As a side note, the Savotta’s rain cover fits the Kahakka quite well, though it is a big baggy. This bagginess does mean it will comfortably cover the pack, even with fully utilized side pouches. Savotta now sells a 30L rain cover which would be more ideal for those interested in a slim line look (or for infrared rating).

The second zipper pocket is a flat pocketA flat pocket is one which does not contain its own volume, but consumes volume from another compartment. In this case, the volume comes from the main compartment. on the front of the pack.

The flat pocket also employs a 2-way zipper (i.e. double-slided zipper), and features the same fabric overhang for weather proofing. It too is difficult to access. If the top lid is buckled closed, access is not permitted. This can be considered a good thing if you want a pocket with additional security. A D-Ring inside is provided for attaching items (like keys) using a carabiner or other clipping system. The pocket can just fit a Kindle Scribe (1st generation 19.6cm x 22.9cm, or 7.72″x9.06″).

Because this is a flat pocket, it fights for space with whatever is in the main compartment. If the main compartment is full, it will be difficult to insert or remove anything from the flat pocket.

Flat pocket (Note: The image has been modified using AI (Nano Banana Pro). There were some fingers left in frame I removed.)

Finally, there are the Kahakka’s “famous” side pouches. I say famous because for every Kahakka review I’ve yet to read, they are considered a surprising treat. And yes, they are large. These are properly 3 liters!

I like them – even if they go against my organizational ideals. In terms of instantly expanding the volume of the pack, they’re fantastic. The pockets don’t have drainnage gromets – but, they do have water drainnage holes! At the corner of each is a small hemmed opening. My only complaint: these drainnage holes are closest to the user, and also don’t make sense from a height point of view. When worn, packs tend to lean from the top (i.e. away from the user, so they aren’t truly vertical), which rotates the pack slightly. Therefore, these holes won’t be at the lowest point they could be, and if water does escape while worn, it is likely to go onto the wearer (although, admittedly, I have not tested.) What I really do like about this design is that unlike grommets, it requires no extra material (less cost, less reliance on other resources) and no added weight.

Kahakka Recommendation: Switch the drainnage hole location to the front of the pack.

Side pouches detail

FILBE

The FILBE features a 2-way zipper pocket on the lower front, with an estimated volume of 6 liters. The zipper, like on the main compartment, is protected with a zipper gasket (a rubberized coating over the teeth). Inside, there is a mesh pockets at the top with a 1-way zipper.

The pocket is large enough for several books, and/or tablet, and/or large laptop chargers, etc. I often used this to hold water as well, as it is easier access than the main compartment when using bottles instead of a bladder.

I wouldn’t change a thing about this, except maybe to make the mesh pocket have a double-slider (and that is just being picky). I just want to reiterate, it is a deceptively small pocket (i.e. seems small but is surprising large), and I am always impressed just how much can be fit inside.

The only thing I don’t like about this pocket is how much PALS webbing is on the face of it. This is unnecessary weight (and manufacturing cost). The amount of PALS webbing the FILBE has lends itself readily to kitting out. But not once have I seen (and I looked!) an additional pouch rigged to the FILBE in this area. And why would you? It would only add unnecessary torque to the user, being the farthest location from the back.

FILBE Front Pocket

FILBE Recommendation: Remove the excess PALS webbing. Remove the middle three of the 5 rows on this pocket to reduce weight and cost.

Straps and Buckles

Shoulder Straps

The FILBE and Kahakka have different size and shape shoulder straps. The FILBE is, in accordance to American designs, wider and thicker. Compared with the Kahakka, the FILBE’s straps are 12mm (0.5”) wider, and 2.5mm (0.1”) thicker.

Kahakka Strap on top of FILBE strap. Sorry colorblind folk...

The Kahakka straps are approximately 60 mm wide (2.26”, measured at the widest point) whereas, the FILBE is approximately 72 mm (2.83”). The Kahakka’s straps are roughly 9.5mm (0.37”) thick while the FILBE’s are 12mm (0.47”).

In terms of comfort, both are good, but the FILBE’s extra width and padding provides it an noticeable edge. I can’t answer at the time of writing this section the difference in comfort while wearing a plate carrier.

Kahakka and FILBE strap side by side

One of the Kahakka’s features are the use of a D-Ring for the shoulder strap attachment. While this doesn’t really allow for true width adjustment of the straps, it can offer some relief in this aspect. In comparison the FILBE’s straps are completely fixed.

Personally, I imagined the difference this D-ring would make in comfort was going to be greater than what was experiened on arrival and with testing. But as an average sized male, I simply didn’t notice any improvement in comfort. However, it can be envisaged that for larger individuals this may make the Kahakka more comfortable as the fixed, non-rotating width between straps of the FILBE might be too narrow for those with wide backs or thick necks. I did find that getting into and out of the backpack is slightly easier with the Kahakka with this rotation ability, as the straps can be swung to a more convenient position.

Kahakka D-Ring Connection (taken from Savotta's online commercial)

One major benefit that the FILBE has over the Kahakka (and notably its parent, the M20) is the shoulder strap’s quick detach mechanism. The padded front straps terminate with SR buckles, allowing the user to instantly remove the backpack. This can be done while in the prone position (or virtually any other), without the user having to rotate or move anything but their hand to the QR buckles. It also means a second person can easily remove the pack from the wearer, such as in a wounded situation, with just two pinches. Should the SR buckles, which also serve as length adjusters for the strap, break, the FILBE comes with back-up, fixed connections.

Given the Kahakka is a commercial pack it’s understandable such a feature isn’t included (though I am inclined to have it). However, as far as I can ascertain from the few published photos, the M20 doesn’t include this quick detach feature, and I think it is certainly worth while.

Kahakka Recommendation : Add a SR buckle to the front shoulder straps.

FILBE QR buckle, and spare fixed buckle

Difficult to determine, but the M20 also appears to not have a QR buckle.

Hip Strap and Buckle

There is one exception to the “bigger and more comfortable” ethos effected by the FILBE: the hip strap. The FILBE’s hip straight measures 38 mm (1.5”) while the Kahakka’s measures 49.5 mm (1.95”). The material thickness are virtually equivalent, but the Kahakka’s strap is noticeably stiffer.

Here the FILBE utilizes a standard QR buckle, but the Kahakka employs a Berg buckle. This is my first experience with a Berg buckle – and I love it. This is a perfect solution for an item which is supposed to be used during high stress environments. Even though standard QR buckles can be opened single-handled, a Berg buckle requires less FMC, and can also be easily opened while wearing winter gloves. The devil’s advocate in me does say that a Berg buckle could be more difficult to unclip in the prone position but I believe this is more of a chaotic neutral feature (sometimes good, sometimes bad – but equally so).

Hip Straps (Kahakka left, FILBE right)

Compression Straps and Buckles

Both the Kahakka and the FILBE have equivalent compression straps, in number and location. The main differences are in the webbing hardware and how excess strap is organized.

Both packs feature 2 compression straps on each side. The FILBE features 2 compression straps on the bottom, but the Kahakka’s equivalent straps compress the bottom, the front, and the top lid.

Front compression straps.

Left side compression straps.

The benefit of this later implementation is more real-estate for extra storaga on the Kahakka – either between the straps and the front of the pack, or beneath the lid. However, this fact is limited by the relatively short length of the straps (69.5 cm or 27.36”) relative to the max volume of the pack. Without a custom adjustment, as will be explained shortly, I was not even able to strap a 3-season duvet sleeping bag (a typical size, smaller than a rugby ball) to the Kahakka.

An additional concern and area for improvement on the Kahakka is that the SR buckles on these front straps are too large to pass through the existing PALS webbing slots. This means custom adjustment requires removing the SR buckle from the strap, pulling the strap out of PALS webbing row(s), then reattaching the buckle. The benefit of this tedious exercise is more room for attaching items (like a sleeping bag) that the tension from the PALS webbing doesn’t permit.

In respect to this PALS dimensioning, the FILBE has widened loops where the straps may pass through (as shown in the photo below). It would be worth while to widen the rows which the compression straps pass on the Kahkka through to permit the buckles to pass through - and this is importantly something Savotta can defintely do.

Kahakka Recommendation: Adjust PALS webbing dimensions to allows SR buckles to pass through.

Kahakka has equal sized PALS loops, which does not permit the SR buckle to pass through.

FILBE has wider PALS loops where the straps pass through, permitting the entire SR buckle plus rolled strap to pass through. This webbing is ~1.4x wider than normal.

The Kahakka’s side straps use G-hooks. They (as far as I can tell) are stamped metal hooks that have been finished to have soft corners. There is something quite elegant about them – and yet, I can’t help but feel like looking at at ideal architect’s home – beautiful, but impractical.

From a manufacturing perspective, they’re great. Instead of requiring 2 parts like an SR buckle, there is only 1 piece required. The hook simply connects over a loop of PALS webbing, which would have already existed there for other functionality. They’re metal and not plastic, so their durability should be even greater than the SR buckles.

But my concerns are in usage. SR buckles can be undone rapidly, and with one hand, though they nearly always require 2 hands to buckle. G-Hooks are the opposite. They can be clasped with 1 hand, but always need 2 hands to unhook. Or rather a hand and a finger, the finger lifting up the PALS webbing to let the hook slide away.

G-hook.

S' bent center bar.

For combat and stressful situations, I firmly hold the belief that unloading is more important than loading, and the one handed unbuckling (SR buckle) is more useful than the one handed hooking (G-hook). Even if one should disagree with this, there is one more thing to consider. Though the G-hook can be attached single handely, it is very difficult (read, virtually impossible except at specific angles) to tighten single handedly. So, the strap length must already be correctly set if you argue that single handed packing is more important than unpacking. Compared to the SR buckles, the adjustment on the G-hooks is an exercise in patience.

I believe Savotta is aware of this drawback, and updated the M20 to the Kahakka some-what accordingly. In the Kahakka, the main compartment is acessed via SR buckles, and not G-hooks, like the M20. In other words, faster access is provided to the main compartment where it might really be needed. I would even bet 2-fingers of Kyrö whiskey that this was learnings from the Ukraine war.

Interestingly, an inspection of the G-hook reveals that the center bar (that which the fabric strap wraps around), is bent in an S-shape, in an orthogonal direction to the plane of the buckle. In other words, it creates 2 small, curved rises, and I believe this improves the the ability for the strap to slide. I don’t actually know why these G-hooks have this ‘S’ feature, and couldn’t find anything about it – so if you’ve an idea, please let me know.

( 04/2026 I have since learned that the S-shape is called a “wave profile” and in fact it is designed to do the opposite of what I thought – it is to enhance the locking of the strap)

In comparison, the FILBE utilizes SR buckles for all compression straps. And they are quite handy for strapping things to both the sides, and below the bag. Unlike the Kahakka’s limited strap length, the underside compression straps of the FILBE are enough to hold a rugby ball sized sleep bag.

FILBE side compression straps with SR buckles.

One final word on straps between the packs are that the FILBE straps all come standard with “strap keeper tabs.” I wasn’t familiar with this term, hence the quotes. On the FILBE these are opposite pairings of velcro, stitched together facing opposite directions. They are inserted into the loop at the end of straps and then used to secure the rolled strap.

Strap Keeper Tab stiched into end-loop.

Strap Keeper Tabs, front and back.

On my 2014 FILBE these were simply slotted through the end-loop and left as is. Unfortunately, either through clumsiness of my own, or through the failing of the velcro hooks with time, these straps entered the domain of Saint Anthony St. Anthony is the Patron Saint of lost items. . My 2025 FILBE however had these stiched in.

This might seem an improvement, and clearly something a pencil-pusher thought of, but the velcro is of poor quality. In other words, these velcro strap keeper tabs won’t get lost anymore, but they will wear out and turn into a fuzzy, unlockable mess, before the bag itself gives out.

Personally, I removed mine and installed higher quality velcro (hence the black strap keeper tabs in my photos.)

Ironically, I think this might be the best use case for G-Hooks. G-Hooks on stretchy bands, not velcro straps. G-Hooks are silent, durable, and rolling up straps is typically not needed in emergency situations but in preparation. The only concern might be the extra weight and cost.

FILBE Recommendation: Replace the strap keeper tabs with high quality velcro, or with compression straps with G-Hooks.

The Kahakka avoids the use of strap keeper tabs in two ways. First, the straps are simply shorter, the limitation being the potential volume of material being strapped to the pack. Second, the PALS webbing can be used on all it’s compression straps to hold the straps in an organized manner. The Kahakkas side PALS webbing is oriented vertically (i.e. the rows run up and down) which is unusual, but permits organization.

Back Panel

The FILBE has a solid flat back, with a slot pocket for the 1cm closed cell foam backer. Unlike virtually the rest of the pack, this slot is made from 500D cordura, meaning the threads are finer. This is likely an unappreciated design choice, as the finer fibers result in less wear on the user’s equipment and clothing. And yes, thicker 1000D will abrade softer materials (i.e. cotton, wool, etc.) over time.

Notably, Savotta decided to make the foam panel easily removable. I have read online reports that grunts like this sort of thing because it gives me a dry and warm placemat to sit on wherever they may find themselves.

It reminds me of when I met and hiked with two Bundeswehr soldiers on vacation by chance. We rested by a river one day, and I promptly sat on a small bolder.

“Don’t do that,” one of them warned. “Sit on cold things will give you hemorrhoids.”

(apparently there is no evidence for this, but I digress. If you have concerns, it seems Savotta already has a solution.)

Kahakka back with removable foam insert partially out.

The FILBE instead features dual closed-cell foam pads which are non-removable. This design provides a channel for the spine to sit it. This central trench, as shallow as it may appear, is effective in getting more air flow and maintaing a cooler back (although TheOutdoorGearReview disagrees with me on this ) To me, the difference between the two packs in this instance is stark.

The FILBE also features double pockets behind these closed-cell foam inserts. In fact, both packs permit the straps and hip strap to be tucked away into these back “pockets.” For the FILBE this is by intentional design as the pack is intended to be mounted atop the main FILBE rucksack (although, it’s not actually necessary). The Kahakka doesn’t share this design intention, and also due to the lack of SR buckles on the shoulder straps, makes this process tedious (although, again, it’s not clear why one might want to, except maybe for sending the pack through hold luggage.)

FILBE back with central channel for air flow. One of the straps is partly tucket in for demonstration.

While the Kahakka relies on the one-piece foam panel to provide structure to the pack, the parall foam pads in the FILBE don’t achieve this. Instead, the FILBE relies on a single plastic sheet which rests in an accessible “pocket” within the main compartment as previously described.

Again, I don’t understand why this was made accessible, but it is. And to be honest, I’m glad it is. First, it provides a secure compartment for documents and cash that isn’t likely to be found under a quick inspection. Second, because of the poor quality control by Propper International, and poor deseign by Eagle Industries.

FILBE plastic insert exposed within the Main Compartment.

To explain – back in the day the surplus FILBEs that were on the market rarely came with the plastic inserts. They were a rarity and as such, they demanded an according price. I came up with my own solution: 4mm polycarbonate cut to shape.

So when my 2025 FILBE was delivered from Propper, I was excited to experience how the FILBE was meant to be be. And I was disappointed. Unfortunately, I did not take pictures. But, the first thing I noticed was that the plastic insert was not cookie-cut (that is to perfect, repeatible dimensions and shape). It was rather evident that someone used a utility knife (i.e. a Stanley blade), and eye-balled the shape out of some large sheet. The insert resembled a trapezoid, and was wavy on two sides. Fortunately it was too large, so trimming was a direct solution.

But the dimensions were the other issue. The insert was both too large, and too thin. It placed unsual pressure on the bag due to its length, and because of its thinness I could see it wearing through the 500D nylon with use as there was clear and constant pressure on the fabric. My solution was simple – wrap some plastic tubing around the sides to increase the width, and trim.

Despite these fixes I maintain that my 4mm polycarbonate is a better solution. It is not only lighter, but thicker proloning the life of the pack, and also provides more support.

Back Insert after trimming.

Back insert with plastic tubing around edges.

Material Qualities and Build Quality

When it comes to Material Quality, both packs use strong fabrics. The Kahakka, officially, uses 1000D Cordura for the core of the backpack, with a piece of 500D for the external foam back plate pocket, as previously described. It has been harder to confirm the fabric for the FILBE, but the most cited figure is 600D, with many sources citing ‘Cordura.’ However, not even Propper provides any material information and even in FAQs only responds with “Nylon.” At best this means a lost marketing opportunity and at worst signals it isn’t infact Cordura or 600D.

For the uninformed, Cordura is an engineered type of Nylon to optimize abrasion resistance and tenacity. Given the same amount of Nylon and Cordura (i.e. mass), Cordura will always outperform the other. The numbering in fabric designations followed by a ‘D’ (e.g. 1000D) is the dernier, or a measure of the linear density of the fiber. In visible terms, the higher the dernier the thicker the individual strands in the fabric will be. Now, a higher dernier doesn’t necessarily mean a higher strength or abrasion resistance, except when comparing like-for-like. For example, 600D run-of-the-mill Nylon is not necessarily stronger than 500D Cordura (in fact, it isn’t). But 600D Cordura is necessarily stronger than 500D Cordura.

Therefore, I want to highlight that yes, while the Kahakka is the smaller pack, it still uses as a principle material one that has nearly twice the weight (1000D vs 600D) as the FILBE’s and manages to remain a 1kg lighter. The PU lining also adds some weight too, but my intuition tells me this increases the tear resistance of the material. So, it is impressive that even with such tough fabric, which wear heavier, the Kahakka remains light.

Considering the fabric alone, the Kahakka is without a doubt more durable. But the bigger difference comes down to the actual build quality.

My 2014 FILBE was great, and if it had not been for a silly accident, I’m certain that it would have lasted many more years to come. But I have since had the experience of trying 3 new FILBEs - 2 from 2025 and 1 from 2026. I have noticed a clear degradation in the manufacturing (…although, again this is perhaps not totally true, as explained below).

For starters, all 3 newer FILBE had the main carrying handle off-center. One would think this was just a mistake if it occured on the first pack, but this is clearly a persistant issue occuring across multiple lots. Given that as of 04/2026 Propper is now charging a whopping $250 – this is simply unbelievable. The problem with an offset carrying handle translates into real-world difficulties when the pack is loaded and heavy. It will cause the pack to rotate in hand because you are not carrying it at a center-of-mass position. It’s not just being persnickety, this is a real world carry problem.

FILBE with offsete carry-handle

Close up of FILBE with off-set carry handle.

What is even more disappointing is that one of the FILBEs that I kept gave out after a few month of usage. I had not even brought this pack camping or filled it with any heavy loads, it was only serving as an EDC, and rarely even at that. Yet, the bottom seam came out. From what I can tell, the fabric ripped out of the seam which must not have had enough material to keep it from doing so.

Tear in bottom seam.

Close up of tear.

So, this brings me to my earlier caveat – has the manufacturing of the FILBE actually degraaded? Back when I bought my 2014 FILBE, there were two manufactuers: Eagle Industries and Propper. Unfortunately, the label was not provided on my surplus so I never had the benfit of knowing which company produced it.

However, based on evidence outside of this review, but provided here When I purchased my 2014 FILBE Assault Pack, separately purchased the main FILBE rucksack. My main pack came with an Eagle Industries tag, and importantly, the fabric coloring on both bags matched. The fabric coloring on the newer FILBE assault packs is different to both 2014 bags – and unlike the earlier matte finish the new ones are shiny. Neither 2014 bag had any issue with the carry handle centering. Finally, the 2014 bags both have cleanly trimmed seam bindings. On all the 2025-2026 bags, the seam binding is wavy as if they have been poorly cut by inexperienced or careless hands. . I am inclined to believe me original FILBE was in fact made my Eagle Industries, not Propper. In short, this is due to the color of the fabric, no issue with the carrying handle, and the difference in the seam binding.

FILBE Recommendation: Propper, to be blunt, get your manufacturing shit together.

I haven’t put my Kahakka to a true endurance test like my 2014 FILBE underwent. But I am absolutely confident in the material and manufacturing. I believe it is one of the highest quality products I have ever owned when it comes to outdoor, hiking, and military gear.

Other Notes - FILBE Assault Pouch

When I first start writing this review (actually more than a year ago!) the cost of the FILBE was ~$25-30 cheaper than the Kahakka. One way to make an equivalent price comparison was adding the “FILBE Assault Pouch,” selling for $30.

Similar to the plastic back stiffener, back in the day this was one of the rare items which one could find, albeit at exorbitant prices, for the FILBE system. Now that it was available for sale, new, I couldn’t pass up the chance.

FILBE side compression straps with SR buckles.

This assault pouch merely adds an additional pocket to the FILBE, with perhaps an additional volume of 1.5-1.75 liters. It is simple. There is just a fabric divider in the middle, and single drainnage grommet. The pouch is accessed by a 2-way zipper, again with weather protection. It’s handy for IDs, keys, etc. In essence anything that needs quick access.

But for $30, it isn’t worth it. First, even when fully attached using the propper PALS weaving technique, it rips off easily – as I experienced first hand on a bus ride and found myself momentarily torn between saving my personal documents or my computer. This is a common complaint for PALS webbing, but it’s the first time I’ve experienced it and I believe it comes down to manufacturing quality. I still have PALS webbing attachment from 20 years ago (yes 20!) that will not rip off, and has nearly the same height dimensions as the assault pouch. Second, because of the dimensions, it makes getting access to the FILBEs true front pocket difficult, especially when the pack is fully. If you absolutely need extra space, it’s definitely adding a pouch here, but not at this quality-to-cost. But I find less value added when the mesh-pocket in the main comparment essentially accomplishes the same job.

Anyway, this conversation is moot for 2 reasons. First, as already mentioned, the price of the FILBE has skyrocketed to $250 (04/2026), a 40% INCREASE in price. All this while the Kahakka has remained at the same pricepoint. And oddly, you can’t even buy the assault pouch from Propper anymore – it’s no longer for sale.

Conclusion and Thougts on Manufacturing

I just want to conclude on a few items, mostly pertaining to the Kahakka. I have a sense that anyone reading this might think I were out to say “FILBE good, Kahakka bad.” And this is not the case.

Both packs clearly have their strengths, and make, what can be argued to be, appropriate trade-offs in terms of materials, construction, and design choices.

Of course, I don’t agree with all of them. I think there are improvements that can be made, without incurring additional costs, risks, or fair loss of functionality.

Regarding the Kahakka, Stefan Meland, a Product Manager at Savotta, said “With a lot of money, you could put together all kinds of superpacks from the US, but will you get them here in Finland in a crisis situation? These are straightforward and reliable goods that are certainly also available, Melander reminds from a security of supply perspective.”

This is very insightful into the thought process behind the FDF’s M20 bag. And from from Savotta’s site, “The Kahakkas are rugged indeed, but we have not sacrificed functionality, nor dumbed down the design, for the sake of durability.”

Yet these two quotes makes me ask some serious questions: Are plastic buckles considered a security weak point from a supply perspective? What about zippers? Are these quotes really being honest – or are they more for marketing?

I want to call “bullshit” on Savotta and Mr. Meland, but in as gentle a way as possible. To me, the greatest weakness of the Kahakka 25L, as an assault pack, is the flip top lid. The lid itself should be kept as an extra pocket and a protective covering. But, the folded-opening underneath should be replaced with a weatherproof zipper, and preferably in a J-Zip style or near full-length zip on both sides (as is done on the M20 Medical pack).

To me, without the zipper, the flip-top lid is a “dumbing down” of the design in order to achieve durability, with a sprinkle of supply security perspective excuse. The Kahakka would be a stronger backpack with improved access.

Now, I am not privy to the same information Savotta or the FDF has in terms of supply chain risk. But, a rapid search reveals there are only 2 companies which engineer zippers in Finland: Teva-Team Oy and Salmi Oy, but neither company does the manufacturing within Finland (or Estonia for that matter). So, maybe zippers are a supply chain risk?

But then, what about Cordura 1000D, the most consumed resource in the Kahakka pack? Nope, there is no manufacturer of Cordura within Finland.

In fact, the only item I managed to find that is actually made in Finland is the G-hook, which is manufactuered by Savotta. I’m not claiming this is the only piece, but it is the only piece I’m aware of.

So, not having a zipper, doesn’t read to me like a supply chain issue – especially when Salmi-Oy has a production facility in Poland (although, it might not be the right zipper type - fair enough). However, let us not forget the M20 Medical Pack does have a zipper. And to me, that is a sign that having a zipper is both acceptable from a supply chain perspective and a ruggedness perspective. Maybe it just costs more for manufacturing each pack as it involves more sewing and production time.

Of course there are some other changes, but these are minor in comparison, and the imagined decision trade-offs can leave me convinced they should remain as they are.

I think the Kahakka 25L is a good pack. I think it can be made into a great one.

And, I am planning to do that in my my current project, found here (NOTE: not yet published).

Concering the FILBE, a pack will only be as good as well as it can be manufactured. It might have, in my opinion the better design, but if it can’t hold up, then it becomes a liability, which can be lethal in combat.
